title: DFT Hidden Gems: Six Concepts Coverage Reports Won't Tell You
description: Lockup latches, chain tests, LOS vs LOC, X-bounding, low-power fill and cell-aware testing: the DFT details that decide whether silicon passes.
content:
Most DFT write-ups stop at "insert scan, run ATPG, check coverage." The concepts that decide whether silicon actually passes test sit one layer below that. Here are six I wish someone had explained to me earlier.

## 1. Lockup latches: the half-cycle that saves your chain

When a scan chain crosses from one clock domain to another, the two clocks rarely arrive at the same instant. If the capturing flop's clock arrives late, the launching flop has already changed its output, and the new value races through. That is a **hold violation during shift**, and it corrupts the chain silently.

A lockup latch sits between the two flops. It is transparent while the launching clock is low, so it holds the data for an extra half cycle:

```verilog
// Transparent while clk_a is low; holds data through the clk_a high phase
always @(clk_a or d)
  if (!clk_a) q <= d;
```

> [!TIP]
> Insert lockup latches at every clock-domain and clock-edge crossing within a chain, not only where STA reports a hold problem today. Clock skew changes after CTS.

## 2. The chain test runs before anything else

Before a single ATPG pattern runs, the tester shifts a pattern like `0011` through every chain and checks it comes out unchanged. This **chain integrity test** (also called a flush test) catches broken chains, stuck scan cells and shift hold problems.

If the chain test fails, every other pattern result is meaningless, which is why it always runs first and why chain diagnosis is its own discipline.

## 3. Launch-on-shift vs launch-on-capture

Transition (at-speed) faults need two clock edges close together: one to launch a transition, one to capture it.

- **Launch-on-shift (LOS):** the last shift edge launches the transition. Coverage is usually higher, but `scan_en` must switch at full speed between that edge and the capture edge.
- **Launch-on-capture (LOC):** `scan_en` drops early and two functional pulses do the work. `scan_en` can be slow, which is why most designs use it.

```wave
# Launch-on-capture: scan_en settles before the at-speed pulse pair
clk     : ppp0..pp0.
scan_en : 1..0......
```

Many teams pipeline `scan_en` so LOS becomes practical without a fast global signal.

## 4. X-sources quietly destroy compression

Unknown values (X) come from non-scan flops, uninitialised memories, floating buses and analog outputs. In uncompressed scan, an X just masks one bit. In a **compressed** flow, X values feed the response compactor, and a single X can corrupt many observed bits in that shift cycle.

The fix is **X-bounding**: forcing known values at the source during test, such as wrapping memory outputs or adding a test-mode mux on a non-scan flop. It costs a few gates and often recovers several points of coverage.

## 5. Fill your don't-cares to save power

ATPG specifies only a small fraction of scan cell values in each pattern; the rest are don't-cares. Random fill toggles flops constantly during shift, and shift power can far exceed functional power, causing IR drop and false failures.

**Adjacent fill** repeats the last specified bit, so long runs shift with almost no toggling:

```python
def adjacent_fill(bits: str, default: str = "0") -> str:
    out, last = [], default
    for b in bits:
        if b in "01":
            last = b
        out.append(last)
    return "".join(out)

adjacent_fill("1XXX0XX1XX")  # -> "1111000111"
```

It trades a little compression efficiency for much quieter shift.

## 6. Stuck-at coverage is not defect coverage

Classic fault models live on cell pins. Many real defects sit **inside** standard cells, such as opens and bridges between transistors that no pin-level fault represents. **Cell-aware testing** characterises each library cell at transistor level and generates patterns for those internal defects. It is one of the reasons automotive programs ask for more than a stuck-at number.

## Quick reference

| Concept | Problem it solves | Where it bites |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lockup latch | Shift hold violations across domains | Post-CTS skew |
| Chain test | Broken or corrupted chains | First pattern on the tester |
| LOS / LOC | At-speed transition coverage | `scan_en` timing |
| X-bounding | Corrupted compressed responses | Memories, non-scan flops |
| Adjacent fill | Shift power and IR drop | High-density patterns |
| Cell-aware | Defects inside cells | Low-DPPM products |

None of these show up in a coverage summary, but every one of them shows up on silicon.
